messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The “standard deviation” you’re looking for is really the **standard error of the sample mean** under the null hypothesis.  
It’s calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
\(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
\(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.221
\]

So the standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean under the null) is **about 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually we compute the standard error: sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. So 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic under null is sqrt((n-1)/(n-2))? Actually t distribution has variance n-1/(n-3) for n>3? Wait, t distribution with df = n-1 has variance df/(df-2) if df > 2. So variance = (n-1)/((n-1)-2) = (n-1)/(n-3). For n=40, df=39, variance = 39/37 ≈ 1.054. Standard deviation = sqrt(1.054) ≈ 1.026. But that's for t distribution. But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They might want the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((sample_std_dev^2 / sample_size) + (population_std_dev^2 / population_size)). But we don't have population std dev. So likely they want the standard error of the sample mean: sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). So answer: 0.221.

But the user might want to use the function "statistics_calculate_p_value" to compute p-value? But they ask for standard deviation. The function calculates p-value. But we can compute standard deviation manually. So we can respond with the calculation: 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. Provide explanation.

Thus answer: standard deviation of the null hypothesis test (standard error) ≈ 0.221.
